title: The "holds up spork" of academia literature
text:
The book is really well put together, organized, and well researched. None of this helps get away from the fact that it's painful to read. I thought the book would catch it's stride eventually, but halfway through it still reads like tumbling down a hill end over end. The work endlessly repeats 'haha look at this funny thing in a research paper, oh look at this thing too so random haha'. Page after page of 2 paragraph synopses of jokes authors sneak into their papers. Reading this feels like I have ADHD, especially with the offensively excessive footnotes which are tactfully used to explain to the reader that Benjamin Franklin is a famous polymath, or to describe the scenery around some arbitrary UK building. In every other case the author takes no shame in using the footnotes to get the last word in on the joke even though he's the primary voice of the book. Good lord I've got a long sense of humor but this reads like a twitter feed.

2/5 good read if you have dementia and can't hold more than 10 lines of information at once.

name: Athan
title: Very funny, hope he completes his PhD
text:
My buddy Jerome and I (separately) read Liar’s Poker in the summer of ’90 so we both ended up at Salomon Brothers a year later. The place was packed with people like us who did not mind wasting their youth trading bonds, because (i) the money was good and (ii) childish behavior was, if anything, encouraged.

We knew we were living in some kind of golden age of misbehaving, so we started compiling a “fun file” of internal memos, emails, company results, axe sheets and publications that we hoped to publish one day. I left in ’97, Jerome in ’99 and the fun file was passed on to our wiser friend Stefan, who retired well before his 50th birthday and intends to publish!

“Academia Obscura” is not quite as good as the original Viz Profanisaurus that is to be found in our fun file (picture attached), but is an extremely thorough compendium of hilarious factoids relating to the much more serious world of academia.

It’s laugh-out-loud funny.

Personal favorites were the author’s views on self-citation (p. 153) and his presentation of important findings regarding socks (p. 177). Before reading this book I’d been led to believe it was gentlemen who are meant to always keep their socks on.

On the other hand, the author tweets the very best bits all the time, and I follow him, so this was a bit like when I went to see “Clerks” and my friend Nick had already told me about the kid that bought the cigarettes, the girl who was allowed to “do everything” by the dead man and “I’m your friend, I got you chicks with…”

So basically, if you already follow Academia Obscura on Twitter, you’ve already read the funniest bits. Then again, if you follow it you probably want to keep all those treasures in one place and a good, old-fashioned book is as safe a way as I know to keep it all in one place. It’s why I've kept my Profanisaurus, at any rate…

name: dairwin
title: No revisions necessary!
text: This book is effectively a compendia of funnies. It is, in places, childish, immature and vulgar. All of these things serve to endear the book to me. As anybody who’s ever spent any time at conferences will tell you, they’re as much about meeting friends (old and new) for conversations which invariably involve much laughter. On the topic of conferences, I to have arrived (and delivered a paper for that matter) while hungover and been involved in a race for one of the few plug sockets (see the book)! It embodies a whole range of topics from the mildly funny to the completely ludicrous. Equally, it is written with a sense of humour. Quite often, when you read about humorous topics, academics have inexplicably managed to suck all the fun out of the topic being considered (much like dementors from Harry Potter – evidence for the paper cited that discusses what if Harry Potter were real). Not so here. Wright weaves an esoteric range of topics together with his own brand of humour and witticisms. It is a wonderfully funny book which, in read in the presence of non-academics my result in black looks when you burst out laughing, followed by blank looks when you try to explain it. Finally, to channel my inner “reviewer 2”, this book spends too much time dealing with scientific papers, and not enough with those for humanities. Also, still channeling said reviewer, Wright’s book is now dated because Twitter no longer uses 140 characters – something which academics, not usually synonymous with brevity, have vehemently condemned (usually using the full 280 characters).

text:

There is no better resource for understanding the cliches that academics use in papers ("Much ado about the null hypothesis"), the backbiting of anonymous peer review, the lengths to which academics go to procrastinate, or homosexual necrophiliac ducks.

Really, just paging through the tables and graphics is worth your time.

Best to read this in the loo, or alternatively, as an excuse for not doing your academic work. And as a dropout from the mathematics Ph.D. program and a purported expert on writing without BSWriting Without Bullshit: Boost Your Career by Saying What You Mean, I know whereof I speak.

You don't need to be an academic to find a lot of this really funny; I read quite a few bits to my family as they kept asking me what I was laughing at. We're still giggling at the Buffalo sentence. It's a relief to find that academics get up to the same kind of daft stuff as the rest of society.

But there's a lot here that will resonate with those who have questioned the logic of what goes on in academia. As I was reading, I often got a sense of 'it's not just me then...'. Almost all of the things that had been niggling at me over the course of my PhD - the ones that you go along with because 'that's how it's done' - have been dissected and ridiculed here: the insane publishing model, the conferences that waste your time and money, the interminable panels, the vindictive peer reviewers and so on. In fact the author would have appreciated the very last conference that I attended, where a keynote (on linguistics) appeared to be an excuse to show slide after slide of close-up penis images. One for the follow-up perhaps?

This is an irreverent look at the inherent humour, craziness and borderline insanity that runs rampant through the academic world. An excellent read for anyone (with a sense of humour) involved in academia!

name: Margaret
text:
I first came across this book via the Twitter account @AcademiaObscura. This is an account that points out the lighter, sometimes absurb, often downright freaking oddball, aspects of life as an academic.

Now I have several academic friends and I have listened to their tales of woe (and student ignorance) at length. Not to mention the fact that I aspired to the academic life myself, though due to circumstances, was unable to reach it. Hell, my English teacher and I already had the title of my first paper worked out! Watership Down: Rabbits and the Traditional Arthurian Quest Motif. The thing is, after reading this book, that putative paper sounds sane and sensible!

I frequently laughed aloud at the sheer ridiculousness of some of the papers mentioned in the book. The scary thing is that the majority were science papers! Though most of the laughs came from the comfortable style, and quirky comments and footnotes of author Glen Wright.

WARNING: This is one book where you MUST read the footnotes. You will miss too much if you don't. Hell, the footnotes alone are worth the price of the book.

A must read for anyone who is an academic, knows an academic, aspires to be an academic, or has a twisted sense of humour.

Now, if you'll excuse me, I think I'll sit here and give some serious thought to actually writing that paper.

name: Savyasachee
text:
Are you an academic? Locked in an ivory tower? Do you have a sense of humour? Pick this book up. An entertaining read about the idiosyncrasies of Homo academicus, this book will definitely brighten up your day. The writer, a PhD student himself, talks about a wealth of topics. Conferences, cats, Shakespeare in science, plagiarism, originality, wit, witticisms, the Oxford comma, nearly everything academics go crazy on has a place in this book.

The slightly dry, whimsical tone of the book really sets the tone for an enjoyable jaunt through academic-fantasy-land. The author does everyone a favour by not taking the subject matter too seriously. Instead, there's open laughter at the number of "Fuck"s published in literature (more than you'd think) and the number of "Cunt"s (none, to the author's surprise), the various reasons academic papers have been rejected, and of course, the one in a million attempts at cartoonishly falsifying data and getting caught.

Keeping to the best traditions of academic publishing, the author liberally sources his work. I must admit I didn't glance through the sources too keenly, so I cannot say whether there's any Easter Eggs hidden in the text or not. I wouldn't be surprised if there were, though. Some day, I'd like to sit down and comb through the sources with a fine-toothed comb and try to see if I can find something to email the author about.

And the best bit about it all? The author is a fellow PhD student! An easy 5/5, would recommend if you have a sense of humour, and would recommend even if you don't. This book will go some ways in developing it yet!

name: Melody Schwarting
text: I bought this on a lark (I think I was purchasing the next semester's textbooks) and it has been a rollicking ride. Beware that it's really about scientific academia--only a few references to the humanities and other disciplinary fields--but it's hilarious all the same. My husband, a research scientist, found it uproarious. I, a non-scientist, deeply enjoyed it. You'll laugh out loud for sure. I definitely recommend it for impostor syndrome and scholarly blues.

name: Henry Percy
text: Summary of some of the stupidist academic research. Author too clever by half. We don't need his "witty" comments telling just how ridiculous the research is. Just the facts, please. Tedious, though it has moments.

name: Rada
text: One of the most hilarious books I’ve ever read — I guess one’s situation (eg, academic life, in this case) is always the best target for sarcasm and fun.

name: JY Tan
text:
This is a fundamentally niche book that will only appeal to academics and those that are on the fence. But to this niche audience, the irreverent writing tone is sorely needed as it communicates two messages that is largely needed: 1. academia is not mysterious and occupied by very real and flawed human beings, 2. academia is often just flat out absurd.

For me this book was entertaining and occasionally thought provoking. The compilation of trivia regarding all things academic made me more comfortable with my work and the community I work in, and in some small ways showed me how can I engage my work more fully and creatively.

The biggest shortcoming of it all is that it does not seem to have a coherent story. The author is frank about this, that ultimately Academia Obscura is really a side hobby that got too serious and accidentally cumulated in a book (like many doctorates and academic careers..). It jumps from proper history of academic writing, publications, and intricacies of going for conferences, to obscure facts about pranks and cats in academia. As a consequence, for how relevant the content is to me personally, this book ends up sadly rather forgettable. I will be reminded of cute facts of the work occasionally, but I don't think I will have more than a few tidbits to share to others if asked 'what stood out to you from this book'.

There is a part of me is of the opinion that this does not need to be a book, staying as a compilation of obscure facts will do the trick. But reading all of this as a whole book achieves something more: it affirms the message that there is something fundamentally flawed and insane about academia, and as we lack proper solutions to these deep seated issues, the best we can do is to sprinkle a fair bit of humor and lightheartedness on top of it all.

name: Stephen Stewart
text: Academia Obscure by Glen Wright explores the hidden humorous, bizarre and unexpected side of academia, looking at topics ranging from academics' love of their pets (and publishing with them too) to all the Easter eggs hidden in published articles. Just having finished by first semester of my PhD, this book was poignant ("publish or perish" is a mantra I've heard several times already) and hilarious with all the things I can do in the future. This book shows that humor is important to hold onto during the rigor of academia, and I think Wright's book does an excellent job showing the hidden silly side of higher education. I'm definitely passing this book to the rest of my cohort.

name: Wouter
text: An excellent read if you want to have a quick laugh at weird people like academics. The sheer brilliance of weirdness made me chuckle out loud more than once. It's funny and quite sad at the same time, and causes me to doubt whether I want to stay in that world or not. Every sector has it's shortcomings and Glen points us towards weird teaching methods, goofy experiences and the use and misuse of publications. It was over too quick, and I doubt I'll remember much after a few months. Amusing but forgettable.

name: S.
text:
Apart from learning some insolite things about Academia, I hold this book in high esteem of being a great punny introduction to what it looks like doing research with an optimistic attitude...

In my case, maybe I should mention this book as a co-author as well, since it brought me laughter and peace essentially needed to undergo any writing process...

"I implore you to own this insanity. Send a silly academic tweet, study an improbable topic, or include a humorous reference in your next paper."

name: Gerda
text:
This was a collection of modern academia related anecdotes. It wasn't bad, but I imagined something different when I bought it. I thought it would be more historical and, well, obscure.
The writing was OK, but the structure could have been better. It was broken down into sections with no real connection between then, except (I guess) that academia can be kind of funny.
I enjoyed some sections more and some less (the twitter section was so bland and redundant I almost stopped reading the book entirely).

name: Asta
text:
Recommended for academics, especially those who don't take themselves too seriously.
Light and funny read.
With lots of references, as appropriate.
And lots of footnotes - not to miss!

"Lightening up has the brilliant benefit of making academia interesting and accessible, and you don't necessarily even need to be that witty or clever to capture people's imagination."

"I hope that I have at least inspired you to embrace humour in your work and to take academia a little less seriously."

name: Vinko Culjak Mathieu
text: Wright's Academia Obscura is a hilarious examination and response to the 'sillier side of higher education'. It highlights the little things that make academia enjoyable and also maddening. It brings to light many problems in academia with a light hearted tone but still gets the reader to think about those problems. A thoroughly enjoyable book that everyone should read, especially those contemplating a career in academia.

name: Ximara
text: Skvělá knížka. Každý, kdo chvíli studoval na jakékoli univerzitě, musel záhy zjistit, že univerzita je úplně jiný vesmír. A to ne jenom kvůli velkému rozdílu mezi střední a vysokou školou, ale především kvůli (díky?) akademikům. Autor humorně, a zároveň odborně rozebírá celý průběh „akademického života“ od publikování přes konference po Twitter. I když jsem četla knihu na můj vkus dlouho, zamilovala jsem si ji. Jistě ji ocení fanoušci komiksu PhD (Piled Higher and Deeper).

name: Maria Rigaki
text: I absolutely enjoyed this book. It gives an insight on the funny and sometime silly side of academia with footnotes and full references while at it! Although it is about academia, one does not have to be an academic to enjoy this book.

name: thefoliofiles
text:
If you are connected to the academia in any way (researcher, student, publisher, family of...), this is a wonderful look into its oddities and eccentricities.
The one book (barring Terry Pratchett's) where I read all the footnotes.

name: Carissa Gomes
title: Really interesting read even for a non-academic
text: It was absolutely informative and amusing. I shared the information acquired with all my friend, Albeit weird. Looking for a part two.

name: Debbie Maclellan
title: Did not meet expectations.
text: Although there are a few funny anecdotes in this book, in general it is not ver funny. I am not sure why there are so many footnotes and why each section of footnotes begins in the same way.
